## June 23, 1956 — A Saturday at the Hinge of Things

You were born on a Saturday in June, in the eleventh year of the post-war world and the fourth year of the Eisenhower presidency. Summer had arrived. Somewhere a radio was playing rock and roll.

---

**You share a birthday with Alan Turing — exactly.** June 23, 1912, was the day the mathematician who invented the theoretical foundations of computing was born. You arrived on the 44th anniversary of that birth, and Turing had been dead for barely two years — he died on June 7, 1954, at 41, under circumstances that remain contested. In June 1956, his name was not widely celebrated; his wartime codebreaking work at Bletchley Park was still classified. He was largely unknown to the public. In your lifetime, he would be rediscovered, rehabilitated, placed on the British fifty-pound note, and recognized as one of the most consequential minds of the twentieth century. The man whose birthday you share theorized the machine you now carry in your pocket before such a machine existed.

**Six days after you were born, Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act.** On June 29, 1956, the president put his pen to legislation that authorized the construction of 41,000 miles of interstate highway — the largest public works project in American history. The country that existed when you were born had a patchwork of two-lane roads; the country you grew up in was being stitched together with concrete at sixty-five miles per hour. The suburbs sprawled along those highways. The American car culture you inherited was in the process of being permanently locked in.

**You were born in the middle of the Montgomery Bus Boycott.** Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat the previous December, and the boycott was in its seventh month when you arrived. It would continue until December 1956 — you were six months old when the Supreme Court ruled that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The civil rights movement that would define the decade of your childhood was already underway, though its most visible confrontations were still ahead.

**The old imperial order was visibly collapsing in the weeks around your birth.** British troops had completed their withdrawal from the Suez Canal Zone on June 13 — ten days before you were born. Egypt was sovereign over the Canal for the first time in decades. Then, five weeks after your birthday, Nasser nationalized the Canal entirely, triggering the Suez Crisis and the last convulsion of British imperial ambition. You were born at the exact moment the post-war world was sorting out who the great powers actually were and would be.

**1956 was the year rock and roll stopped being a rumor.** Elvis Presley had released "Heartbreak Hotel" in January and it had gone to number one. "Don't Be Cruel" and "Hound Dog" — on the same single — were coming that summer. Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino: the cultural earthquake that would reshape popular music for the rest of the century was peaking in the months around your birth. You were born into the year the old sound broke.

**The Cold War was the weather.** The Soviet Union and the United States each had hydrogen bombs by the time you were born, and both sides knew what those weapons meant. Civil defense drills, the threat of Soviet missiles, the arms race conducted in the upper atmosphere — this was the permanent background radiation of your childhood.

---

**The arc of 70 years.**

You were born into a country where almost no one had encountered a computer, where television had been in wide use for less than a decade, where the tallest building in the world was the Empire State Building, and where most Americans had never boarded a commercial jet.

You turned thirteen the summer humans walked on the Moon. You came of age as Watergate dismantled a presidency in real time on television. You watched the Berlin Wall fall in your early thirties. You saw the internet move from military network to global commons to the organizing system of daily life. You watched a phone become a camera, a map, a library, a newspaper, and a video studio small enough to fit in a shirt pocket.

And Turing's birthday-twin lived to see the machines he theorized not merely built but made conversational — systems that reason, write, and argue, arriving in the last chapter of a lifetime he shared, by birthdate, with the man who first proved they were possible.

That is the distance June 23, 1956 covers. Seventy years from Eisenhower signing the highway bill to artificial intelligence writing poetry. Not a bad span to have witnessed.
